description: Infinity Physics leverages Physics, Health, and AI to solve complex scientific challenges. Track record: 21st with High Honors globally (out of 1,955 teams), Top 10 in Pharaohs' Fragments, and 5th in the Egyptian Olympiad in Computational Science.
summary:
We developed an autonomous, onboard space health and mission monitoring framework engineered for deep space exploration. At its core is a 6 qubit Quantum AI model built on NASA GeneLab RNA seq data (OSD 1010 and GLDS 815) that compresses 250 radiation sensitive human gut biomarkers into quantum feature space. By leveraging quantum state mapping, the system overcomes small orbital sample sizes to detect early cellular radiation stress from heavy ions (Iron 56 and Silicon 28) and distinguish protective probiotic (LGG) immune activity from true radiation damage in real time.
To address the broader challenges of deep space, where communication delays prevent real time Earth medical support, our platform integrates three additional modules: cross gravity machine learning models forecasting bone, muscle, liver, and retinal adaptation across lunar and Martian regimes; an offline Isolation Forest pipeline tracking personal circadian baselines, cabin CO2, and crew cognitive physiological signals (EEG, ECG, and PPG); and a graph theory food supply predictor.
This solution is vital for upcoming lunar and Martian missions, shifting space medicine from reactive external sensors to proactive, personalized crew protection.
details:
Deep space exploration beyond low Earth orbit exposes astronauts to compounding biological and operational hazards, including galactic cosmic radiation, partial and microgravity regimes, prolonged isolation in closed habitats, and communication delays with Earth that make real time ground medical support impossible. To address these challenges, we developed an autonomous, onboard space health and mission logistics decision support framework engineered to run locally on spacecraft systems. Rather than relying on passive external radiation badges or generic population averages, our platform integrates quantum machine learning, biophysical modeling, unsupervised physiological monitoring, and graph theory logistics to deliver early, personalized risk assessments and actionable countermeasure timelines for upcoming lunar and Martian expeditions.
At the center of our biological monitoring architecture is a two layer Space Radiation module built on open NASA GeneLab human gut on chip RNA sequencing datasets (OSD 1010 and GLDS 815). In the first layer, raw transcriptomic profiles spanning 37,968 genes across 19 clean samples are filtered down to the 250 most radiation sensitive biomarkers and compressed into quantum feature space using a 6 qubit Quantum AI classifier. By mapping complex gene interactions onto six core quantum indicators, the model overcomes the statistical limitations of small orbital datasets to generate real time medical risk percentages, accurately distinguishing healthy baseline cellular activity (3.60% risk) and beneficial Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG (LGG) probiotic immune activity (30.07% risk) from harmful Silicon 28 (78.38% risk) and heavy Iron 56 (82.85% risk) radiation exposure. Complementing this quantum classifier, a second biophysical dose response layer analyzes 16 clean samples across 16,707 active genes (refined from 57,500 raw genes via DESeq2 normalization and empirical Bayes shrinkage) to evaluate five critical biological pathways: p53 DNA stress, inflammation, interferon signaling, cell proliferation, and gut barrier integrity. Using both Linear and Poisson Hit nuclear track equations, the model transparently bounds predicted gene activity shifts at unmeasured low doses, such as projecting a +2.0% to +10.1% rise in p53 stress at 0.1 Gy, while clearly separating high confidence Iron 56 findings (34 significant genes, replicate correlation r = 0.33) from exploratory LGG results (1,554 responsive genes, n = 2) and lower confidence Silicon 28 or extrapolated high dose estimates.
To forecast multi organ adaptation across planetary destinations, our Gravity Field module leverages spaceflight and ground analog datasets from the NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR), including GLDS 111 and OSD 557. Through strict, leakage free preprocessing pipelines, Multi Layer Perceptrons (MLP), dual head neural networks, and ensemble regressors simulate physiological trajectories across Earth (1.0g), Mars (0.38g), the Moon (0.16g), and microgravity (0.0g). Evaluated across four biological systems, the framework captures distinct tissue degradation timelines: in skeletal muscle (GLDS 111), a dual head neural network achieves 100% held out classification accuracy (ROC AUC = 1.000), pinpointing key atrophy biomarkers such as Eif4ebp1 and projecting that postural soleus muscles reach a critical 20% mass loss threshold by Day 50 in microgravity, Day 76 on the Moon, and Day 159 on Mars. Simultaneously, hepatic ensemble models project liver lipid accumulation escalating from 5.38% on Earth to 12.37% on Mars, 14.88% on the Moon, and 16.68% in microgravity, while bone mineral density models (R2 = 0.5705) reveal heightened vulnerability in metabolically compromised phenotypes (a 6.93% loss in space and 4.33% on Mars compared with 2.24% in normal controls), and residual covariance simulations of retinal tissue (OSD 557) enable individualized ocular risk profiling.
Safeguarding astronaut health inside closed habitats also requires continuous, offline monitoring of environmental and neurophysiological stability. Our Isolation and Crew Cognitive Monitoring framework addresses this in two stages. First, an autonomous onboard anomaly detector learns each astronaut's personal 7 day hourly circadian baseline across heart rate, SpO2, skin temperature, sleep quality, and cabin CO2 rather than relying on generic population averages. Using an unsupervised Isolation Forest to compute a continuous 0 to 100 risk score, and requiring risk to remain above 60 for three consecutive hours before triggering an alert, the system detected 100% of simulated emergencies across a 30 day mission record (cabin CO2 spikes, infection like episodes, and acute sleep loss) with 17 false alarm hours, while pinpointing the exact driving signals behind each alert and evaluating wearable sleep quality prediction on the open MMASH dataset (n = 22, MAE = 1.62 versus 1.69 baseline). Second, for real time flight operations, a multimodal fusion pipeline processes raw 20 channel electroencephalogram (EEG) and electrocardiogram (ECG) recordings alongside peripheral vital signs (heart rate, SpO2, pulse, and respiration from the BIDMC dataset) over sliding 10 second windows. Combining 33 brain and heart spectral, entropy, and variability features with 17 vital sign metrics into a 50 feature vector, a participant specific Isolation Forest with a 3 window persistence filter analyzed 3,913 windows across four simulated flight tasks to trigger 95 tiered alerts (Advisory, Warning, and Critical) for cognitive fatigue and hypoxia, validated via One Class SVM cross checks and equipped with an automatic fallback mode whenever ECG signal quality degrades.
Because deep space crews depend on finite, difficult to replace consumables, our fourth module introduces a web based Food Supply Monitoring and Prediction System paired with an interactive graph theory simulator. The inventory ledger enforces strict data integrity by rejecting negative quantities, duplicate entries, and incompatible measurement units, while a recency weighted moving average of per crew consumption, adjusted for resupply events and onboard greenhouse production, forecasts the exact number of days remaining until minimum reserve thresholds and total stock depletion. Visual dashboards separate historical measurements from future projections, raise early reserve warnings, and support CSV data import and export. To make life support vulnerabilities intuitive for crews and mission planners, an accompanying interactive game models the galley, storage, dining, recycling, and greenhouse modules as a directed weighted graph, applying shortest path algorithms, cycle detection, and cut vertex analysis to expose bottlenecks and single points of failure.
Developing this unified ecosystem required combining Python scientific computing libraries (NumPy, Pandas, SciPy, and Scikit learn) with quantum circuit simulation frameworks (such as Qiskit or PennyLane) for our 6 qubit quantum classifier, deep learning libraries (PyTorch or TensorFlow) for neural network modeling, DESeq2 bioinformatics pipelines for RNA sequencing shrinkage, digital signal processing filters for EEG and ECG telemetry, and web technologies (HTML, CSS, and JavaScript) for the interactive inventory and graph theory platform. The creativity of our project lies in bridging traditionally isolated disciplines, uniting quantum feature mapping, multi organ biophysical forecasting, offline circadian anomaly detection, and playable network topology into a single onboard copilot engineered for low latency inference on spacecraft computers and wearable sensors. Throughout development, our team carefully accounted for real world orbital constraints, including small biological sample sizes, sensor motion artifacts, and model uncertainty. By enforcing leakage free validation, multi window persistence filtering, automatic sensor fallbacks, and explicit separation between measured spaceflight data, interpolated ranges, and synthetic demonstration logs, our platform establishes a transparent, scalable foundation for proactive space medicine and mission resilience on the Moon, Mars, and beyond.
